title.narrative: Strengthening Civil Courage – External Stress Factors / International Lobby and Advocacy

description.narrative: In the Strengthening Civil Courage programme, the pillar of work called External Stress Factors (ESF) is aimed primarily at taking away stress factors that are external to the conflict. The conflicts in which the alliance is seeking to implement its programme have a myriad of external stress factors. For the international lobby and advocacy component of the work on external stress factors, the alliance seeks to address the factors caused by two types of actors: states and companies. Impact through environmental factors is also part of the programme.

The activity is part of a larger programme implemented by the Strengthening Civil Courage Alliance, consisting of ABAAD – Resource Center for Gender Equality, Amnesty International The Netherlands, DefendDefenders, PAX and their partner networks.

The main objective for this programme is that states, companies and other actors contribute to effective international standards which protect people against harm caused through the effects of weapons, business activities in conflict-affected areas or environmental impacts of conflict. More specifically, the programme aims for states to contribute to effective international standards regulating the use of and trade in (controversial) weapons; and, for companies to adhere to effective international standards that prevent and mitigate human rights impacts of businesses in conflict. Lastly, the programme aims to address and mitigate environmental impact of warfare.

The programme targets states, the Dutch government, the UN and multilateral bodies, arms companies, affected communities, financial institutions, multinational companies, and consumers in Western countries.

title.narrative: Outcome 2.1 Financial institutions have systems and mechanisms in place to prevent, mitigate and remediate adverse human rights impacts of their investments in companies producing weapons or involved in human rights violations.

# of financial institutions that have systems and mechanisms in place to prevent, mitigate and remediate adverse human rights impacts of their investments in companies producing weapons or involved in human rights violations (SCS 2)

comment.narrative: 0 EU financial institutions have improved systems and mechanisms
Up to 15 EU financial institutions have improved systems and mechanisms

2021: 1 FI has published a revised policy on Remedy; 1 FI has added controversial arms dealers to its exclusion list 2022: Between 2020 and 2022, 15 financial institutions in the Netherlands improved their investment policies to prevent, mitigate and remediate impacts of investments in companies involved in human rights violations. Ultimately, this should lead to pressure on their investee companies or clients to prevent, mitigate and remediate human rights violations as well. This change trajectory could take place through divestment or engagement (critical dialogue) with the company. There is no reason to change course, but it is important that other FI’s, also outside the Netherlands, make similar improvements. (ESF014 and ESF015)

title.narrative: Output 1.1.1 - Research publications and advocacy initiatives on the direct, indirect and reverberating harm resulting from EWIPA feeds into international discussions on the issue.
# of research publications and advocacy initiatives on the direct, indirect and reverberating harm resulting from EWIPA feeds into international discussions on the issue. (SCS 4)

comment.narrative: 10 research publications and accompagnying advocacy initiatives have been produced by PAX over the past years
4 research publications and advocacy initiatives on the direct, indirect and reverberating harm resulting from EWIPA fed into international discussions on the issue.

2021: 1 blog on the reverberating effects of EWIPA in Hawija (https://paxvoorvrede.nl/nieuws/berichten/blog-inwoners-gebombardeerd-hawija-we-dachten-dat-de-missie-ons-zou-beschermen) , 1 publication on the civilian impact from incendiary weapons and investments in their producers (https://paxforpeace.nl/media/download/PAX_REPORT_Put%20Out%20the%20Fire_FINAL_digital_singlepage.pdf) 2022: In November 2022, 83 states signed the Political Declaration on strengthening the protection of civilians from the humanitarian consequences arising from the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. Through signing the declaration, states a.o. commit to implement policies and practices to avoid civilian harm by restricting or refraining from the use of explosive weapons in populated areas. Furthermore they commit to collect, share and make publicly available disaggregated date on the direct and indirect effects on civilians, and to provide assistance to victims and their communities. PAX has been an active founding member of the International Network on Explosive Weapons (INEW). Through research on the impact and reverberating effects of explosive weapons in populated areas (for instance in Iraq and Ukraine), PAX contributed to the evidence based advocacy that fed into the state process leading to this declaration. In addition, PAX’ policy publications and advocacy with parliament, MFA and MoD likely contributed to the Netherlands signing the declaration as well. In 2022, PAX published 3 report or advocacy initiatives. (ESF001, ESF002, ESF003, ESF004) 2023: INEW held side events during the PoC week at the UN in New York, as well as during 1st committee, and held regional briefings, see: https://www.inew.org/events/regional-briefing-for-african-states/ and https://www.inew.org/events/side-event-strengthening-the-protection-of-civilians-from-explosive-weapons-in-populated-areas/, and https://www.inew.org/events/poc-week-side-event-on-protecting-civilians-from-explosive-weapons-in-populated-areas/ 2024: EWIPA advocacy: Active participation the Oslo conference on the political declaration, including organization of the Protection Forum, a ful day focus on civilian harm in advance of the Oslo conference, attended by states and civil society, exhibitions, drafting and delivering statements, public event screening of For Sama documentary, and PAX participation from both Yemen partner as Ukraine PAX representative. Presentations in serveral ocasions, including a UNIDIR workshop in March in Geneva for states and cicil society on qualitative data research on civilian harm from EWIPA. Research publication on the impact from EWIPA on the environment in Ukraine. Several media interviews on landmines and cluster munitions.

title.narrative: Outcome 1.1 States contribute to international standards aiming to prevent civilian suffering from EWIPA and the use of drones and placing robust limits on arms exports, including drones, to high risk countries.
# of States and international bodies explaining their arms export policy in the context of the Arms Trade Treaty (ATT) (SCS 2)

comment.narrative: Most states are highly reluctant to explain or discuss concrete export policies within the ATT.
Discussing specific arms exports in plenary ATT contexts has become an accepted norm.

2021: Due to Covid restrictions, there was very limited meeting time, not allowing for elaborations beyond general statements 2022: In Geneva in August 2022 Dutch and other EU government officials elaborated during an Arms Trade Treaty side event how they assessed risks of transferring weapons to Ukraine, in light of the war and risk of diversion. Until then, for eight years, besides individual exceptions, discussions on risk assessments by government officials for concrete cases had not happened during (margins of) ATT meetings. This strengthens the existing international standard of the ATT: as states show (even limited) transparency about their considerations around arms transfers, this pressures other signatory states to follow suit. Increased transparency in the context of the ATT would in the long run ensure that states comply with the notion in the ATT that arms should not be exported if there is an overriding risk they will be used in violations of human rights and IHL. (ESF021) 2023: 3 States (Australia, Canada and Georgia) + EU on behalf of all 27 states mentioned Russia's aggression against Ukraine as reason not to supply weapons to them, and/or to urge others not to do so. Palestine highlighted transfers to israel in the context of violations of int.law against Palestine. 2024: Arms trade: EU on behalf of all 27 states + 8 aligning themselves, mentioned Russia's aggression against Ukraine as reason not to supply weapons to them and to allow for transfers to Ukraine. On several occasions Palestine highlighted transfers to Israel in the context of violations of int.law in Gaza. This was amplified by a statement by the Maldives on behalf of the 57 member states of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Also several European states (incl. NL and UK) as well as Israel, Japan, Turkey and Brazil made statements on this in a national capacity. EWIPA: Over 90 states attended the first international follow up conference after the signing conference of the political declaration on explosive weapons. States came from all regions of the world and include producers of explosive weapons, past users of explosive weapons in populated areas, and countries that are affected by armed conflict.

title.narrative: Outcome 2.3 Multinational companies active in conflict-affected areas adopt heightened due diligence mechanisms in conflict-affected areas
# companies that endorse heightened due diligence mechanisms (SCS 2)

comment.narrative: There has not been a VPI plenary meeting decision on heightened due diligence.
1 Voluntary Principles Initiative Plenary meeting decision on heightened due diligence for companies with operations in conflict areas.

2021: The Dutch government announced that it will start working on national level human rights due diligence legislation, which should contribute to the number of companies developing heightened due diligence. 2022: A conflict analysis tool and Guidance document was produced by the VPI Conflict WG and endorsed by 32 multinational companies. This was implemented as planned: PAX took the initiative on this guidance document and ensured the VPI working group produced the tool. With a significant number of high risk companies (32) endorsing the tool, we are on track for our planned change process of making conflict analysis standard part of the due diligence procedures of companies operating in conflict affected and high risk areas. The outcome is completed, no reason to change course. (ESF025)
